questions.question: The foreign exchange reserve of India dropped to levels that were ______ during 1991 economic crisis.

options.text: not sufficient for even fifteen days

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**not sufficient for even fifteen days**__**.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **foreign exchange reserve of India** in 1991 dropped to a critical level, which was **not sufficient for even a fifteen-day**** **worth of imports.
 
• This crisis was a result of **high fiscal deficits**, **rising oil prices** due to the Gulf War, and a significant **balance of payments deficit**.
 
• India's reserves had depleted to a mere **$1.2 billion**, which was inadequate to cover its essential imports, creating an economic emergency.
 
• To tackle this crisis, the Indian government had to approach the **International Monetary Fund (IMF)** for a bailout and pledged its gold reserves as collateral.
 
• This economic crisis eventually led to the introduction of the **1991 Economic Reforms**, including **liberalization, privatization, and globalization (LPG reforms)**, which significantly transformed the Indian economy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Causes of the 1991 Economic Crisis:**

 
 
• **High fiscal deficit:** The government's expenditure far exceeded its revenues, leading to unsustainable fiscal imbalances.
 
• **Oil price shock:** The Gulf War in 1990-91 caused a sharp rise in global oil prices, putting additional pressure on India's import bill.
 
• **Balance of Payments (BoP) crisis:** India faced a severe BoP crisis due to a sharp decline in foreign exchange reserves.
 
• **Mounting external debt:** India's external debt was unsustainable, and servicing this debt became increasingly challenging.
 
 
 
• **Measures Taken to Resolve the Crisis:**
 
 
• **Pledging gold reserves:** India pledged **67 tonnes of gold** to the Bank of England and other financial institutions to secure loans.
 
• **IMF bailout:** India sought a loan from the IMF under its **Structural Adjustment Program** to stabilize the economy.
 
• **Economic reforms:** The government initiated a series of reforms under the leadership of **Dr. Manmohan Singh**, then Finance Minister, to liberalize the economy.
 
 
 
• **1991 Economic Reforms:**
 
 
• **Liberalization:** Removal of licensing requirements and restrictions on industries to promote private sector participation.
 
• **Privatization:** Disinvestment of public sector enterprises to improve efficiency and reduce the fiscal burden.
 
• **Globalization:** Opening up the Indian economy to foreign investment and international trade.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Reforms:**
 
 
• **Economic growth:** Post-1991, India's GDP growth accelerated, and the country emerged as one of the fastest-growing economies.
 
• **Increased foreign investment:** The liberalization of the economy attracted significant foreign direct investment (FDI).
 
• **Export growth:** Indian industries became more competitive globally, leading to an increase in exports.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Foreign Exchange Reserves:** These are assets held by a central bank in foreign currencies, used to back liabilities and influence monetary policy.
 
• **Balance of Payments (BoP):** It is a statement that summarizes a country's economic transactions with the rest of the world over a specific period.
 
• **Structural Adjustment Program:** A set of economic policies imposed by the IMF or World Bank as a condition for financial assistance to stabilize and reform the economy.
 
• **Fiscal Deficit:** It represents the gap between the government's total expenditure and its total revenue, excluding borrowings.

questions.question: IPv4 address is a string of numbers consisting of four parts, where each part is a number between _________ and _________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**0, 255**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• IPv4 address is a string of numbers consisting of four parts, where each part is a number between 0 and 255.
 
 
• An **Internet Protocol address (IP address) **is a numerical marker that identifies a computer network that employs the Internet Protocol for communication.
 
• An example of such an IP address is **192.0.2.1**.
 
• Identification of the **network interface and location addressing **are the two primary purposes of an IP address. 
 
• An IP address is a **32-bit number according to Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4)**.
 
• Some of these are designated for special uses, such as **multicast addressing (270 million addresses) and private networks (18 million addresses)**. 
 
• **Dot-decimal notation** is the most common way to express IPv4 addresses.
 
• It consists of **four decimal values, each ranging from 0 to 255**, separated by dots, for example, 192.0.2.1.
 
• Each component represents an **octet**, or **8-bit section**, of the address. 
 
• Technical writing may occasionally use different** hexadecimal, octal, or binary representations **of IPv4 addresses.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Since an IPv4 address can only be 32 bits long, there are **only 4294967296 (232) addresses **in the address space.
 
• However, a new version of **IP (IPv6), **utilising **128 bits** for the IP address, was established in **1998** in response to the expansion of the Internet and the exhaustion of IPv4 addresses.
 
• Deployment of IPv6 has been happening since the **middle of the 2000s**.
 
• **Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA)**, a global organisation, and five regional Internet registries **(RIRs)** oversee the management of the IP address space
 
• **IANA distributed IPv4 addresses to the RIRs in blocks of roughly 16.8 million** addresses each, however, the supply has been **depleted at the IANA level since 2011**.

questions.question: Which among the following does NOT directly influence population change?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Employment**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Population change** is primarily influenced by three factors: **fertility rate**, **mortality rate**, and **migration.** These are considered direct contributors to changes in population numbers.
 
• **Fertility rate:** This refers to the average number of children born per woman during her lifetime. Higher fertility rates lead to population growth, while lower rates contribute to population decline. *Hence, this influences population change directly.*
 
• **Mortality rate:** The number of deaths per thousand people in a population. A higher mortality rate reduces population numbers, while lower mortality rates contribute to population growth. *Thus, it directly affects population change.*
 
• **Migration:** Movement of people from one region to another, either internationally or within a country. Migration can increase or decrease population in specific areas. *Hence, it directly impacts population change.*
 
• **Employment:** While employment opportunities can encourage migration, which in turn indirectly affects population distribution in certain regions, it does not directly influence overall population change. Employment does not increase or decrease the total number of people in the population. *Hence, it does NOT directly influence population change.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Fertility Rate:**

 
 
• The **fertility rate** is a critical demographic indicator. For example, in many developing countries, the fertility rate is high, contributing to rapid population growth.
 
• The **Total Fertility Rate (TFR)** of a country often indicates its population growth trends. As of recent data, countries like **Niger** have a TFR above 6, while nations like **Japan** have a TFR below 2.
 
 
 
• **Mortality Rate:**
 
 
• The **infant mortality rate** and **life expectancy** are closely monitored to assess population health. For instance, countries with better healthcare systems often have lower mortality rates.
 
• The global average mortality rate has decreased over the years due to improvements in healthcare, sanitation, and nutrition.
 
 
 
• **Migration:**
 
 
• Migration can be **voluntary** (e.g., for better job opportunities) or **forced** (e.g., due to war or natural disasters).
 
• For example, the **Syrian refugee crisis** led to significant migration to European countries, influencing population dynamics in host nations.
 
 
 
• **Employment:**
 
 
• Employment is often a pull factor for migration. Urban areas with better job opportunities attract people from rural regions, influencing regional population distribution but not overall population size.
 
• For instance, cities like **Mumbai** and **Delhi** in India have seen a significant rise in population due to migration driven by employment opportunities.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Population Change Factors:**

 
 
• Fertility and mortality rates are natural factors, whereas migration is a social factor affecting population dynamics.
 
• Employment indirectly affects population distribution but is not a direct factor influencing total population change.
 
 
 
• **Demographic Trends:**
 
 
• **High fertility rates:** Typical in developing regions (e.g., Sub-Saharan Africa).
 
• **Low fertility rates:** Observed in developed nations (e.g., Europe, Japan).
 
• **Migration:** Often driven by economic opportunities, political stability, and environmental factors.

questions.question: Which of the following techniques was used to make stone tools in ancient India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Pressure Flaking**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Pressure Flaking** is a technique used in ancient tool-making where a sharp instrument, such as a bone, antler, or wood, is used to apply pressure to the edge of a stone core to remove small flakes and shape the tool.
 
• This method was used to create sharp edges and refine tools like arrowheads, spearheads, and knives, making them more efficient and precise for hunting or cutting.
 
• **Pressure Flaking** was a significant advancement compared to earlier methods like direct percussion, as it allowed for greater control over the size and shape of the flakes removed.
 
• It was particularly prominent during the **Mesolithic and Neolithic periods**, where more sophisticated tools were needed for activities such as farming and hunting.
 
• The tools created using this method were generally smaller and sharper than those made using older techniques, reflecting the evolution of human craftsmanship and technological skills.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Step Flaking:**

 
 
• This technique involves striking the stone at specific angles to create a "step" pattern. It was primarily used in the Paleolithic period to create larger, less refined tools.
 
• Step flaking often resulted in uneven surfaces and was less precise compared to pressure flaking.
 
 
 
• **Bipolar Technique:**
 
 
• In this method, a stone core is placed on a hard surface and struck from above, causing it to split. It was used to create smaller flakes and tools.
 
• This technique is often associated with the production of microliths in later prehistoric periods.
 
 
 
• **Pecking:**
 
 
• Pecking involves striking a stone repeatedly with a harder stone to shape it. This technique was used to create larger tools, such as axes and hammers.
 
• It was more common in the Neolithic period when polished tools became essential for activities like agriculture.
 
 
 
• **Evolution of Stone Tool Technologies:**
 
 
• Stone tool-making techniques evolved from basic percussion methods in the Paleolithic era to more refined methods like pressure flaking in the Mesolithic and Neolithic periods.
 
• This evolution reflects the increasing complexity of human societies and their need for specialized tools to meet different challenges.
 
 
 
• [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 
• **Pressure Flaking** was essential for creating tools with fine edges required for specific tasks, such as cutting, scraping, or drilling.
 
• This technique highlights the ingenuity of early humans and their ability to innovate with available resources, marking a major step in the development of human technology.
 
• Archaeological evidence of pressure flaking has been found in regions such as Africa, Europe, and India, showcasing its widespread use.

questions.question: The phenomenon of bending light when it passes through one transparent medium to another is due to _________________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**4) Refraction**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Refraction** is the bending of light as it passes from one transparent medium to another with a different optical density, such as air to water or glass.
 
• This phenomenon occurs due to the change in the speed of light when it enters a medium with a different refractive index.
 
• Refraction is responsible for common optical effects, such as the apparent bending of a stick partially submerged in water.
 
• The angle of incidence and the angle of refraction are related by **Snell's Law**, which states: *n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂*.
 
• Applications of refraction include lenses in eyeglasses, cameras, microscopes, and telescopes, as well as natural phenomena like rainbows and mirages.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Refractive Index:**

 
 
• The refractive index of a medium is the ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to the speed of light in that medium.
 
• It determines how much light bends when entering or exiting the medium.
 
 
 
• **Snell’s Law:**
 
 
• It mathematically describes the relationship between the angles of incidence and refraction and the refractive indices of the two media.
 
• Formula: *n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂*, where *n* is the refractive index, and *θ* is the angle.
 
 
 
• **Critical Angle and Total Internal Reflection:**
 
 
• The critical angle is the angle of incidence above which total internal reflection occurs instead of refraction.
 
• This principle is used in optical fibers for efficient light transmission.
 
 
 
• **Dispersion of Light:**
 
 
• Refraction causes dispersion, where white light splits into its constituent colors, as seen in a prism.
 
• This occurs because different wavelengths of light refract at slightly different angles.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Refraction:**
 
 
• Used in designing lenses for vision correction, optical instruments, and cameras.
 
• Essential in understanding natural phenomena like mirages, rainbows, and the twinkling of stars.

• **Bacterial ooze** is a characteristic feature of certain plant bacterial diseases. This ooze is often sticky, slimy, and may appear as a discolored liquid or exudate from infected plant tissue.
 
• It occurs due to the breakdown of plant cells caused by bacterial activity. This breakdown releases cell contents, which combine with bacterial colonies to form the ooze. *This is a defining characteristic of bacterial infections in plants.*
 
• Bacterial ooze is commonly observed in diseases like **bacterial wilt** (caused by **Ralstonia solanacearum**) and **fire blight** (caused by **Erwinia amylovora**). These diseases affect crops like tomatoes, potatoes, apples, and pears.
 
• In contrast, viral and fungal diseases, or nematode infestations, do not typically produce bacterial ooze. Viral diseases cause systemic symptoms like mosaic patterns or stunted growth, while fungal diseases result in spore formation and mycelial growth. Nematode infestations often lead to root damage but not bacterial ooze.
 
• *Hence, the presence of bacterial ooze is an identifying feature of bacterial diseases.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Bacterial Diseases in Plants:**

 
 
• **Bacterial wilt:** Caused by **Ralstonia solanacearum**, it affects crops like potatoes, tomatoes, and bananas. Symptoms include wilting and bacterial ooze when stems are cut.
 
• **Fire blight:** Caused by **Erwinia amylovora**, it primarily affects apple and pear trees. The disease causes branches to appear scorched, and bacterial ooze may be visible on the bark or fruits.
 
• **Soft rot:** Caused by **Pectobacterium** species, it results in tissue maceration and bacterial ooze in vegetables like carrots and potatoes.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Pathogens:**
 
 
• **Viral diseases:** Caused by viruses, these diseases show mosaic patterns, yellowing, or stunted growth. No bacterial ooze is present in viral infections.
 
• **Fungal diseases:** Fungi produce spores and mycelial growth instead of bacterial ooze. Examples include powdery mildew and rust diseases.
 
• **Nematode infestations:** Nematodes are microscopic worms that damage plant roots, leading to root galls or stunted growth. They do not cause bacterial ooze.
 
 
 
• **Prevention and Management of Bacterial Diseases:**
 
 
• Use of disease-free seeds and resistant plant varieties.
 
• Crop rotation to prevent the buildup of bacterial pathogens in the soil.
 
• Application of copper-based bactericides or antibiotics (where permitted) to control bacterial infections.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Diagnostic Methods for Bacterial Diseases:**

 
 
• Cutting infected plant stems under water to observe bacterial ooze.
 
• Microscopic examination of bacterial colonies from infected tissues.
 
• Molecular techniques like PCR for accurate identification of bacterial pathogens.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Bacterial Diseases:**
 
 
• Bacterial diseases significantly reduce crop yield and quality, leading to economic losses in agriculture.
 
• Early identification and management are crucial to prevent disease spread.

questions.question: Which method is adopted to prevent soil erosion in hilly area?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Terrace farming.**__

__**Explanation:**__

__
 
• **Terrace farming** is the **practice of growing crops on the sides of hills or mountains** by planting them on graduated terraces carved into the slope, or in other words, the practice of carving flat areas out of hilly or mountainous terrain to grow crops.
 
• They can **reduce surface run-off and prevent soil erosion in hilly areas.**__
 
• Terrace cultivation is **practiced in the Indian states of Punjab, Meghalaya, Haryana, the Plains of Uttar Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh, and Uttaranchal.**
 
• Terrace farming is used to grow paddy, cereals, fruits, vegetables, flowers, medicinal plants, aromatic plants, dye plants, wheat, maize, rice, pulses, oilseeds, and other crops.

Thus, __**terrace farming method is adopted to prevent soil erosion in hilly area.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/73346acc7a17fbed82607f23313db8a23af96e59a0102c3076a6eb66e68d6258.png]

• Increased sloping field farmability and production.
 
• By slowing and reducing water run-off, it improves rainwater collection and contributes to water conservation.
 
• Reduces rill forms, which prevents soil erosion.
 
• Water pollution and sedimentation are reduced.
 
• Adapts hilly land for cultivation in order to increase food output.

questions.question: Which material was most commonly used to make Harappan seals?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Soapstone**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Harappan seals were primarily made of **soapstone**, also known as steatite, a soft stone that could be easily carved into intricate designs.
 
• Soapstone was often treated with heat, which gave it a hardened and glossy finish, making it durable and aesthetically appealing.
 
• These seals typically featured engravings of animals, humans, and inscriptions in the Harappan script, which remains undeciphered to date.
 
• The seals were used for multiple purposes, including trade, authentication, and administrative activities, acting as a form of identification or trademark.
 
• Soapstone was widely available in the region during the Harappan period, making it a preferred choice for manufacturing seals.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Terracotta:**

 
 
• Terracotta refers to baked clay and was extensively used by the Harappans for creating figurines, pottery, and toys.
 
• Although terracotta objects were common in Harappan civilization, it was not the material of choice for making seals due to its fragility and inability to hold fine details.
 
 
 
• **Copper:**
 
 
• Copper was widely used in Harappan culture for tools, weapons, and ornaments but not for seals.
 
• The metal's properties made it suitable for practical tools rather than intricate carvings like seals.
 
 
 
• **Faience:**
 
 
• Faience is a glazed ceramic material made from crushed quartz. It was used by Harappans to craft beads, bangles, and other decorative items.
 
• Although faience was significant in Harappan craftsmanship, it was not typically used for making seals due to its delicate nature.
 
 
 
• **Harappan Civilization:**
 
 
• The Harappan civilization, also known as the Indus Valley Civilization, existed around 2600–1900 BCE and was known for its advanced urban planning, trade, and craftsmanship.
 
• The seals, made primarily from soapstone, reflect the high level of artistic and technical skills of the Harappans.

questions.question: The inputs used in the production of goods or services to make an economic profit are known as _________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**factors of production.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• The **inputs** utilized in the** creation of goods or services **to generate a profit are referred to as** factors of production.**
 
• These include all materials required for producing a good or service.
 
• **Land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship** are the production factors.
 
• The overall factors of production can be impacted by the** status of technical development,** which can also account for any **efficiencies **not directly related to the four traditional components.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Four factors of production**—land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship.
 
• **Land:**
 
 
• Every **natural resource utilized** to produce goods and services is included in land.
 
• **Water, oil, copper, natural gas, coal, and forests** are a few examples.
 
• The** raw materials used in the industrial process **are land resources. These resources can be both **renewable and nonrenewable.**
 
 
 
• **Labor:**
 
 
• The** effort that people put forth** to produce goods and services is referred to as labor. 
 
• The** income earned** by labor resources is called **wages** and is the largest source of income for most people.
 
 
 
• **Capital:**
 
 
• Consider capital as the **equipment, tools, and buildings **that people utilize to produce commodities and services.
 
• Depending on the worker and the sort of job being done, capital varies.
 
• **Interest **is the source of income for owners of capital resources.
 
 
 
• **Entrepreneurship:**
 
 
• An entrepreneur is a person who uses **capital, labor, and other production elements** in combination to turn a profit.
 
• **Profit **is how entrepreneurship gets compensated.

questions.question: Price ceiling refers to:

__
 
• A** price ceiling** is a sort of **price regulation** that establishes the **maximum price **a seller may charge for a good or service and is typically imposed by the **government.**
 
• These are often imposed on necessities like **food, gas, or medicine**, frequently following a **crisis or specific occurrence** that causes prices to soar.
 
• The** benefits** of a price floor include maintaining **affordable pricing, preventing price gouging, and growing demands.**
 
• Price floor **disadvantages **include** frequent supply shortages, the potential for quality loss and cost-cutting**, as well as the possibility of** additional fees or higher costs** for other commodities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Price Floor:**

 
 
• A price floor, which establishes a **minimum cost for purchasing** a good or service, is the opposite of a price ceiling.
 
• It stands for the** lowest legal price** at which a good or service may be offered and still adhere to the basic laws of supply and demand.
 
• This is also known as "**price support."**
 
 
 
• **GST:**
 
 
• An** indirect tax **on the provision of goods and services is known as the GST, or **Goods and Services Tax. **
 
• It is a **multi-stage, destination-oriented tax** imposed on every value addition, replacing multiple indirect taxes, including VAT, excise duty, service taxes, etc
